sections.title: Framing the history: cell lines and anaemia

blocks.text: Most blood problems come down to **one cell line being made in excess or in short supply** (red cells, white cells or platelets). Build the history around which line is abnormal and in which direction. In the routine systems review, screen with four questions: **easy bruising or bleeding, tiredness, lumps (nodes), and abdominal fullness** (a hint of a big spleen).

blocks.title: What to ask when a count is high or low
rows: Headache, blurred vision; hypoxia (smoking, lung disease) or dehydration as secondary causes; look for a raised white count with basophils; JAK2 for primary polycythaemia
Breathlessness, fatigue, chest pain; are white cells also low (marrow failure)?; trend over time; diet history (vegans take little iron and B12)
Recent infection (reactive neutrophilia); allergy, asthma or eczema (eosinophils); blood film for immature cells (malignancy)
Infections (cause or effect), mouth ulcers, family history, careful drug history; benign neutropenia in young women; neutropenic sepsis needs rapid IV antibiotics
Headache, itch, bleeding (very high counts bleed); infection or cancer, since secondary thrombocytosis is commoner; splenomegaly suggests a myeloproliferative disorder
Petechiae, blood blisters; recent viral illness (ITP), rheumatological disease, drugs; bleeding with operations, labour and dental extraction

blocks.title: Symptoms of anaemia
items: Non-specific: **tiredness, weakness, breathlessness**, headache, palpitations, faintness or postural dizziness.
Anaemia can unmask or worsen **angina, heart failure or intermittent claudication**, especially in the elderly.
Grade severity by asking how far the patient can walk on the flat or how many stairs they can climb before getting breathless.
Specific to iron deficiency: **pica** (craving non-foods such as soil) and hair loss.

blocks.title: History clues to the cause of anaemia
rows: GI loss: melaena, haematemesis, ulcer or colitis, NSAIDs or anticoagulants; full GI history; in women, heavy periods (menorrhagia is a common premenopausal cause)
Alcohol; diet (vegan diet → B12 deficiency); gastrectomy (loss of intrinsic factor) or terminal ileal resection (B12 not absorbed)
Aspirin/NSAIDs → blood loss; sulphonamides → haemolysis; chloramphenicol → marrow aplasia
Chronic malaria or intestinal parasites cause much chronic anaemia worldwide

blocks.text: Speed matters: anaemia that develops **quickly** (e.g. bleeding) causes far more symptoms than a slow fall in Hb, which the body compensates for, so a patient may be symptom-free. Coexisting heart or lung disease also makes patients more symptomatic.
Always ask an anaemic patient about **chest pain**: severe anaemia can worsen ischaemic heart disease and may need urgent treatment.
Anaemia and chronic leukaemias are usually found on a **routine blood count**, not at the bedside. The history earns its keep by pointing to the **cause**.

In a patient who seems to bleed too much, the history answers three questions: **(1)** is there a generalised haemostatic defect? **(2)** is it inherited or acquired? **(3)** does the pattern point to a **vascular/platelet** problem or a **coagulation factor** problem? Bleeding from several sites, spontaneous bleeding, or bleeding out of proportion to an injury all suggest a generalised defect.

blocks.title: Bleeding history checklist
items: Site(s) and duration of bleeding; age at onset.
Precipitants: surgery or trauma. **Dental extraction, tonsillectomy, circumcision**, childbirth and operations are natural stress tests of haemostasis.
Family history of bleeding, drug history, and other illness such as liver disease.

blocks.title: Platelet/vascular versus coagulation bleeding
rows: Petechiae, many small bruises, mucosal bleeding (nose, gums, mouth)
Haemarthroses, deep muscle haematomas, retroperitoneal or intracranial bleeds

blocks.title: Inherited bleeding disorders
items: **Haemophilia A** (factor VIII) and **B** (factor IX) are **X-linked recessive**. Severe disease bleeds spontaneously into weight-bearing joints (especially knees) and large muscles, leading to arthropathy.
**Von Willebrand factor** (gene on chromosome 12) anchors platelets to exposed collagen and protects factor VIII. Von Willebrand disease is **autosomal dominant** with incomplete penetrance.

Severe inherited defects usually declare themselves in infancy (sometimes as prolonged bleeding from the umbilical stump). Mild ones may only appear after surgery, childbirth, dental work or trauma, or on a preoperative screen.

blocks.text: A **negative family history does not exclude** an inherited bleeding disorder: about **one-third** of haemophilia cases have no family history, and deficiencies of factors VII, X and XIII are recessive.

Repeated bleeding from **one site** points to a local structural lesion rather than a coagulopathy. Normal screening tests do not exclude **von Willebrand disease or scurvy**, so the clinical history carries the weight.

blocks.title: Thrombosis history
items: Acquired venous risk factors: obesity, older age, smoking, oral contraceptive or HRT, pregnancy, immobility, orthopaedic or pelvic surgery, cancer, heart failure, IBD, vasculitis.
Inherited/immune: factor V Leiden, prothrombin gene mutation, antiphospholipid syndrome, protein C, protein S or antithrombin deficiency.
**Factor V Leiden plus the oral contraceptive** raises thrombotic risk roughly **100-fold**.

Haematological causes of **arterial** thrombosis: polycythaemia, sickle cell anaemia, heparin-induced thrombocytopenia and thrombosis (HITT), SLE, antiphospholipid syndrome, inherited protein C or S deficiency.

blocks.title: Anticoagulant history
items: Which agent: heparin, warfarin (INR checks and target range) or a DOAC (apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran).
Any bleeding complications; any vena caval filter or surgery for clot.

sections.title: Malignancy, infection, treatment and background history

blocks.title: Symptom patterns of haematological disease
rows: Enlarging nodes plus **B symptoms** (fever, weight loss, night sweats) and tiredness. Hodgkin may add itch, cough, breathlessness and node pain after alcohol
**CRAB**: hypercalcaemia (calCium), Renal impairment, Anaemia, Bone pain or fractures; also recurrent infections and a large tongue from amyloid
Fatigue, fever, pallor, petechiae, unusual bruising or bleeding, nodes, hepatosplenomegaly (failure to thrive in children); request an urgent FBC
Itch (pruritus), headache, blurred vision; ask about smoking and chronic lung disease (secondary, hypoxic causes)
May be silent, or cause fatigue, weight loss, sweats, fever; abdominal discomfort from a big spleen, thrombosis, bleeding, a red face, infections

blocks.title: Recurrent infection as the first clue
items: Leukaemia (neutropenia), myeloma (reduced normal immunoglobulins), HIV (lymphopenia), primary immunoglobulin deficiency (recurrent sinusitis and chest infections).

blocks.title: Lumps: history of a node
items: Speed of onset and growth, pain, and associated weight loss, sweats or itch.
**Reactive** nodes usually swell quickly and hurt; nodes from haematological malignancy are more often **painless**.
Not every lump is a node: consider lipoma, abscess (tender, fluctuant), sebaceous cyst (in the skin), thyroid nodule, or a reactive node after immunisation or cellulitis.

blocks.title: Treatment history and what it implies
rows: Haemophilia; ask older patients about hepatitis and HIV status

blocks.title: Family, ethnic and social history
items: Thalassaemia: Mediterranean or southern Asian origin. Sickle cell disease: African origin.
Benzene exposure or previous chemotherapy raises the risk of leukaemia and myelodysplasia.
Alcohol intake.

blocks.text: Patients often forget **over-the-counter drugs such as aspirin**. Ask specifically, because many medicines cause blood problems.

Exam key-word patterns: petechial rash in a well patient → **ITP**; pallor and fatigue with low Hb and low MCV → **iron deficiency**; prolonged fever, nodes and hepatosplenomegaly → **lymphoma**; falling Hb with reticulocytosis and diffuse pain → **sickle cell anaemia**.

sections.title: Inspection: general, hands, face, mouth and skin

blocks.title: General inspection
items: Wasting, **pallor**, racial origin, bruising, **jaundice** (haemolysis), scratch marks (lymphoma, myeloproliferative disease), cyanosis or **plethora** (polycythaemia), pigmentation.
Eyes: scleral jaundice, pallor, haemorrhage, or prominent scleral vessels (polycythaemia).

blocks.title: Signs in anaemia
rows: Mucous membrane/conjunctival pallor, tachycardia, tachypnoea, raised JVP, systolic flow murmur, ankle oedema, postural hypotension, heart failure
**Koilonychia** (long-standing), angular stomatitis/cheilitis, atrophic glossitis, brittle hair and nails

blocks.text: **Conjunctival pallor** is the most reliable bedside pallor sign: more useful than nail-bed or palmar-crease pallor. Palmar crease pallor suggests Hb **below about 70 g/L** but is unreliable. Remember anaemia is never a final diagnosis: always look for the cause.

blocks.title: Hands
items: **Koilonychia**: spoon-shaped, brittle nails of severe iron deficiency.
Digital infarcts: abnormal globulins such as cryoglobulinaemia.
Rheumatoid hands: **Felty syndrome** = rheumatoid arthritis + splenomegaly + neutropenia (may also have thrombocytopenia, haemolysis, pigmentation, leg ulcers).
Gouty tophi: may reflect myeloproliferative disease (high cell turnover).

blocks.text: Long-term **phenytoin** causes gum **hypertrophy**, not gum bleeding. Gum bleeding fits aplastic anaemia, scurvy or haemophilia.

blocks.title: Purpura and bruising
rows: Platelet or coagulation defects, trauma, steroids, ageing skin
Systemic **vasculitis** or bacteraemia, not thrombocytopenia; HSP affects buttocks and legs
Around hair follicles of the legs

blocks.text: Platelet thresholds differ by purpose. Talley lists thrombocytopenia (< 100 × 10⁹/L) as a cause of petechiae, but **Davidson** says spontaneous bleeding usually needs a count **< 20 × 10⁹/L** unless platelet function is also impaired, and **< 10 × 10⁹/L** risks retinal and intracranial bleeding. Follow Davidson for the bleeding threshold.

A non-blanching petechial rash has a dangerous differential: **meningococcal septicaemia**, leukaemia, vasculitis, HSP, ITP and non-accidental injury. A child or young adult with petechiae or hepatosplenomegaly needs immediate hospital referral.

blocks.note: Look at: the overview with insets for koilonychia, glossitis and angular stomatitis, AML gum hypertrophy, petechiae, fundal haemorrhage, toe gangrene with thrombocytosis and a haemophilic joint.
Look at: thrombocytopenic petechiae (compare Fig. 21.5, ecchymoses, and Fig. 21.3, digital infarction).
Look at: Henoch–Schönlein purpura, raised purpura over the legs.

blocks.title: Technique and node groups
items: **Neck**: sit the patient up and examine from behind. Eight groups: submental, submandibular, jugular chain, supraclavicular, posterior triangle, postauricular, preauricular, occipital.
**Axilla**: five groups: central, lateral, pectoral (medial), infraclavicular and subscapular (lowest).
**Epitrochlear**: flex the elbow to 90° and feel just above and slightly in front of the medial epicondyle. Enlargement is usually pathological (local infection, NHL, rarely syphilis).
Also the **inguinal** nodes, and search the area each enlarged group drains.

blocks.title: Describing a node
rows: Localised (look at the drainage area) vs generalised
Fixed to deep structures or skin → malignancy

blocks.title: Node features that predict serious disease (LR+)
Supraclavicular nodes
items: **Left** supraclavicular node (**Troisier sign**): metastasis from chest, abdomen (especially **stomach**) or pelvis.
**Right** supraclavicular node: malignancy from the chest or oesophagus.
The scalene node lies between the two heads of sternomastoid.

blocks.text: Small cervical nodes are often palpable in **healthy young people**, but **posterior cervical** nodes are almost never normal.
Lymphoma nodes are typically **painless and rubbery**; **lymph node biopsy** makes the diagnosis. CLL gives **generalised** lymphadenopathy.

blocks.note: Look at: the eight cervical and supraclavicular node groups numbered 1–8, with photos of cervical and submandibular lymphadenopathy.

sections.title: Spleen, abdomen and completing the examination

blocks.text: The spleen enlarges **downwards and medially**, following the line of the **10th rib** towards the **right iliac fossa**, so start palpating in the RIF and work up to the left costal margin. To catch a small spleen, wrap your left hand around the lower left ribs to lift them forward, and roll the patient onto their **right side**. A normal spleen is about **11 cm** long and is palpable only when substantially enlarged; ultrasound or CT confirms it.

blocks.title: Spleen or left kidney?
rows: Palpable notch on the leading (medial) edge
Superficial, comes out from under the costal margin
You cannot get above it under the ribs
Dull (no resonant band of bowel over it)

blocks.title: Percussion for a spleen
items: **Castell spot**: lowest left intercostal space in the anterior axillary line; dullness on full inspiration suggests splenomegaly.
**Traube space**: bounded by the 6th rib, the midaxillary line and the left costal margin.
LR+: palpable spleen **8.2**; Traube dullness 2.3; Castell spot 1.2. Palpation is the best sign.

blocks.title: Causes of splenomegaly
rows: CML, myelofibrosis, (CLL); chronic malaria, kala-azar; rarely Gaucher disease or primary splenic lymphoma
Haemolysis, haemoglobinopathies, leukaemias, lymphomas, myeloproliferative disorders
Portal hypertension, storage disease, amyloidosis, neoplasia, tropical splenomegaly

blocks.text: **Hypersplenism** can follow splenomegaly of any cause (blood disease, portal hypertension, Felty syndrome, lymphoma). It produces **pancytopenia**, haemolysis from pooling of red cells, and an expanded plasma volume.

blocks.title: Completing the examination
items: Abdomen: hepatomegaly, ascites, masses; para-aortic nodes strongly suggest lymphoma.
**Bones**: tap the spine with a fist and press the sternum, clavicles and shoulders; tenderness suggests marrow expansion (myeloma, lymphoma, carcinoma).
**Legs**: ulcers above the malleoli (sickle cell, spherocytosis, thalassaemia, polycythaemia, Felty); B12 neurology (neuropathy, subacute combined degeneration); haemophilic joints.
**Fundi**: hyperviscosity (macroglobulinaemia, myeloproliferative disease) gives engorged retinal veins, later papilloedema; haemorrhages with thrombocytopenia or other haemostatic disorders.
Finish with the **temperature chart** and **urinalysis**.

blocks.text: **Splenomegaly** is the most consistent physical sign in **CML**. In ITP the spleen is palpable in only about **20%**, so a big spleen argues against ITP. Splenic infarction gives severe left upper quadrant pain to the left shoulder tip with a splenic rub.

blocks.note: Look at: bone marrow aspiration and trephine biopsy from the posterior iliac crest under local anaesthetic, with smear, karyotype and trephine core.

cards.front: Two symptoms specific to iron deficiency (beyond general anaemia symptoms)?
cards.back: Pica (craving non-foods such as soil) and hair loss

cards.front: Three history points in a macrocytic anaemia?
cards.back: Alcohol; diet (vegan → B12 deficiency); gastrectomy or terminal ileal resection

cards.front: Haematological effect of sulphonamides vs chloramphenicol?
Bleeding immediately after surgery vs delayed bleeding: which defect each?
cards.back: Immediate → platelet plug (primary haemostasis) defect; delayed → coagulation factor defect

cards.front: What fraction of haemophilia has no family history?
Factor V Leiden plus the oral contraceptive: change in thrombotic risk?

cards.back: **CRAB**: hypercalcaemia, renal impairment, anaemia, bone pain/fractures (plus recurrent infections)
Fever, weight loss, drenching night sweats

cards.front: Palmar crease pallor suggests Hb below what level?
cards.back: About 70 g/L, but it is unreliable; conjunctival pallor is better

cards.front: Platelet count below which spontaneous bleeding usually occurs? Retinal/intracranial risk?

cards.back: Enlarged left supraclavicular node: metastasis, classically from the stomach

cards.front: Node feature with the highest LR+ for serious disease?
Five features that identify a spleen rather than a left kidney?
cards.back: Notch; superficial; cannot get above it; dull to percussion; moves with respiration
Lowest left intercostal space, anterior axillary line (dull on full inspiration = splenomegaly)
CML, myelofibrosis (CLL); chronic malaria, kala-azar; rarely Gaucher

questions.theme: Clues to the cause of anaemia in the history
questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.
options: Iron deficiency from gastrointestinal blood loss
Vitamin B12 deficiency from a vegan diet

items.stem: A 58-year-old man with knee osteoarthritis has taken ibuprofen every day for two years. He is tired, gets breathless walking uphill, and twice last month passed black, tarry stools.
items.explanation: NSAID use plus melaena points to gastrointestinal blood loss, the usual cause of iron deficiency in a man.

items.stem: A 61-year-old woman had a total gastrectomy for gastric cancer six years ago. She now has fatigue, tingling in both feet, pallor and a raised MCV.
items.explanation: Removing the stomach removes intrinsic factor, so B12 cannot be absorbed. Macrocytosis and neuropathy fit B12 deficiency.

items.stem: A 25-year-old woman was started on co-trimoxazole for a urinary infection. Four days later she is pale and jaundiced and her urine is dark.
items.explanation: Two steps: co-trimoxazole contains a sulphonamide, and sulphonamides can cause haemolysis, which gives jaundice and dark urine.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man has a hot, swollen, painful right knee after a minor tackle at football. He has had similar episodes in both knees since childhood, and a maternal uncle had the same problem. There are no petechiae.
questions.leadIn: Which type of haemostatic defect does this history most suggest?
options: Local structural lesion of the joint
questions.explanation: Bleeding into joints (haemarthrosis) in a male, with an affected maternal uncle, is the classic coagulation-factor pattern of X-linked haemophilia. Platelet and vascular defects give skin and mucosal bleeding instead.
whyNot: Platelet function defects cause petechiae, small bruises and mucosal bleeding, not haemarthroses.
Thrombocytopenia causes petechiae and mucosal bleeding rather than bleeding into joints.
Scurvy causes perifollicular purpura and gum disease, not recurrent haemarthroses from childhood.
A local lesion bleeds from one site; this involves both knees and has a family pattern.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man is treated with unfractionated heparin for a deep vein thrombosis. Seven days later his platelet count has fallen by more than half and his left leg becomes cold and pulseless from an arterial occlusion.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Arterial thrombosis with a falling platelet count during heparin therapy is HITT, one of the haematological causes of arterial thrombosis.
whyNot: ITP causes bleeding, not arterial thrombosis.
Vitamin K deficiency lowers clotting factors and causes bleeding, not thrombosis or low platelets.
Haemophilia A is an inherited bleeding disorder presenting from childhood.
Von Willebrand disease causes mucosal bleeding, not arterial occlusion.

questions.theme: Haematological diagnoses suggested by the history
questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man has three months of back pain, thirst and constipation. Blood tests show a raised creatinine and a low haemoglobin, and he has had two chest infections this winter.
items.explanation: Two steps: thirst and constipation suggest hypercalcaemia; with renal impairment, anaemia, bone pain and infections this completes the CRAB pattern of myeloma.

items.stem: A 23-year-old woman has had drenching night sweats, generalised itch and 8 kg of weight loss over three months. A painless lump in her neck aches after she drinks wine.
items.explanation: B symptoms, itch and node pain after alcohol are typical of Hodgkin lymphoma.

items.stem: A 60-year-old long-term smoker with chronic lung disease complains of headaches, blurred vision and generalised itching. He looks ruddy.
items.explanation: Itch, headache and a plethoric face suggest polycythaemia; smoking and chronic lung disease are hypoxic secondary causes to ask about.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman has spoon-shaped, brittle fingernails, a smooth sore tongue and painful cracks at the corners of her mouth.
questions.leadIn: Which deficiency is most likely?
questions.explanation: Koilonychia is the discriminating sign of long-standing iron deficiency; angular stomatitis and atrophic glossitis fit too.
whyNot: Vitamin C deficiency gives gum swelling or bleeding and perifollicular purpura, not koilonychia.
B12 deficiency can cause glossitis but not koilonychia; look for neurological signs instead.
Folate deficiency can cause glossitis but not spoon-shaped nails.
Vitamin K deficiency causes bleeding from clotting-factor deficiency, with no nail or tongue signs.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man has fever, joint aches and painful, raised purple spots on his legs and buttocks. His platelet count is 260 × 10⁹/L and clotting tests are normal.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely explanation of the rash?
questions.explanation: Raised (palpable), painful purpura is not caused by low platelets; it suggests systemic vasculitis (or bacteraemia). HSP characteristically affects the buttocks and legs.
whyNot: The platelet count is normal, and thrombocytopenic petechiae are flat, not raised.
Scurvy gives perifollicular purpura and gum changes, not painful raised lesions with fever.
Haemophilia causes joint and muscle bleeds, not palpable purpura, and clotting tests would be abnormal.
He is not on warfarin and clotting tests are normal.

questions.theme: Interpreting a lump in a lymph node area
questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.
options: Metastatic carcinoma from the chest or oesophagus

items.stem: A 63-year-old man has lost weight and feels full after small meals. There is a hard, fixed node just above the medial end of his left clavicle.
items.explanation: Two steps: a hard, fixed left supraclavicular node is Troisier sign, and the upper GI symptoms point to the stomach.

items.stem: A 19-year-old student is well. Her doctor finds two soft, mobile, non-tender 0.5 cm nodes in the anterior neck.
items.explanation: Small cervical nodes are often palpable in healthy young people; under 1 cm, soft and mobile, they are usually normal.

items.stem: A 35-year-old man has painless, rubbery 3 cm nodes in the neck and axilla and has had night sweats for two months.
items.explanation: Rubbery, painless nodes with B symptoms suggest lymphoma; biopsy confirms it.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man has a mass in the left upper quadrant. You need to decide whether it is the spleen or the left kidney.
questions.leadIn: Which finding most supports the mass being the spleen?
options: A notch is felt on its medial edge
A resonant band is heard over the mass on percussion
It enlarges downwards towards the left iliac fossa
Your hand can get between the mass and the costal margin
It is felt deep in the loin rather than superficially
questions.explanation: A palpable notch is characteristic of the spleen. The spleen is also superficial, dull, enlarges towards the right iliac fossa, and you cannot get above it.
whyNot: A resonant band of overlying bowel suggests the kidney; the spleen is dull.
The spleen grows down and medially towards the right iliac fossa.
You cannot get above the spleen under the ribs; getting above a mass suggests the kidney.
The spleen is superficial; a deep loin mass suggests the kidney.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man has fatigue, sweats and weight loss. His spleen is felt from the left costal margin across to the right iliac fossa. The white cell count is very high.
questions.leadIn: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Massive splenomegaly with a very high white count is classic CML; splenomegaly is its most consistent sign.
whyNot: In ITP the spleen is palpable in only about 20% of cases, and ITP is not a cause of massive splenomegaly or a very high white count.
HHT causes telangiectasia and bleeding, not splenomegaly.
Haemophilia causes joint and muscle bleeds, not splenomegaly.
Iron deficiency does not cause massive splenomegaly or a raised white count.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 70-year-old man with Waldenström macroglobulinaemia has headache and blurred vision. What is fundoscopy most likely to show?
items.explanation: Macroglobulinaemia causes hyperviscosity, which engorges the retinal veins and can progress to papilloedema.

items.stem: A 50-year-old man has had nosebleeds for years and now has iron deficiency anaemia. His father had the same problem. Which sign should you look for around his mouth?
items.explanation: Inherited recurrent bleeding with iron deficiency suggests hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia; look for telangiectasia on the lips and tongue.

items.stem: A 19-year-old man with sickle cell disease is examined. Which sign on the lower legs is typical of his condition?
items.explanation: Ulcers above the malleoli occur in haemolytic anaemias such as sickle cell disease.

items.stem: A 72-year-old man who lives alone on tea and toast has swollen, bleeding gums and tiny bleeds around the hair follicles of his shins. Which skin sign is almost diagnostic of his condition?
items.explanation: Two steps: a diet with no fruit or vegetables causes vitamin C deficiency, and perifollicular purpura is almost diagnostic of scurvy.

questions.stem: A medical student is examining patients for anaemia in a clinic.
questions.leadIn: Which bedside sign is the most reliable pointer to anaemia?
questions.explanation: Conjunctival pallor is more reliable than nail-bed or palmar crease pallor; its presence is useful, though its absence does not exclude anaemia.
whyNot: Nail-bed pallor is an unreliable sign.
Palmar crease pallor suggests Hb below about 70 g/L but is also unreliable.
Tachycardia is non-specific and has many causes.
A flow murmur is non-specific and appears mainly in more severe anaemia.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with immune thrombocytopenia asks when she is likely to start bleeding spontaneously. Her platelet function is otherwise normal.
questions.leadIn: Below which platelet count does spontaneous bleeding usually begin, according to Davidson?
questions.explanation: Davidson: spontaneous bleeding usually needs a count below 20 × 10⁹/L, and below 10 × 10⁹/L there is a risk of retinal and intracranial haemorrhage.
whyNot: 150 × 10⁹/L is around the lower limit of normal; no bleeding is expected.
Talley uses < 100 × 10⁹/L to define thrombocytopenia as a cause of petechiae, but spontaneous bleeding usually occurs only at much lower counts.
50 × 10⁹/L is low, but spontaneous bleeding is not usual at this level.
Bleeding usually begins well before the count falls this low; < 10 × 10⁹/L is the threshold for retinal and intracranial bleeding risk.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman develops a deep vein thrombosis three months after starting the combined oral contraceptive pill. Her mother had a pulmonary embolism at 30.
questions.leadIn: Which inherited abnormality, combined with the pill, raises thrombotic risk about 100-fold?
questions.explanation: Factor V Leiden is an inherited thrombophilia; with oral contraceptive use, thrombotic risk rises about 100-fold.
whyNot: Haemophilia carriage is a bleeding tendency, not a thrombophilia.
Von Willebrand disease causes bleeding, not thrombosis.
Factor XIII deficiency is a recessive bleeding disorder.
HHT causes bleeding from telangiectasia, not venous thrombosis.

questions.stem: You find an enlarged lymph node in a 58-year-old patient and want to judge how likely it is to reflect serious disease such as lymphoma.
questions.leadIn: Which feature has the highest positive likelihood ratio?
questions.explanation: A fixed node has an LR+ of about 13, the highest of the listed features.
whyNot: Hard texture has an LR+ of about 3.3.
A supraclavicular site has an LR+ of about 3.1.
Size > 9 cm² has an LR+ of about 8.4, high but below a fixed node.
Age over 40 has an LR+ of about 2.25.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man has followed a strict vegan diet for eight years. He has fatigue and numb feet. He is pale with a smooth tongue and reduced vibration sense in both feet; his MCV is raised.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely cause of his anaemia?
questions.explanation: Step 1: the raised MCV makes this a macrocytic anaemia, so the history should cover alcohol, diet and gastrointestinal surgery. Step 2: the diet history is the key clue: vegans take in very little B12. Step 3: the examination backs it up: glossitis plus a peripheral neuropathy (and possibly subacute combined degeneration) are B12 features. Remember to examine the legs for B12 neurology in any macrocytic anaemia.
whyNot: Iron deficiency gives a low MCV and koilonychia, not a raised MCV with neuropathy.
CKD anaemia is usually normocytic, with oedema, hypertension or excoriations, and does not cause neuropathy.
Thalassaemia trait gives a low MCV and is suggested by Mediterranean or southern Asian origin.
Haemolysis would give jaundice and splenomegaly, and does not explain the neuropathy.

questions.stem: In an OSCE you are asked to examine a patient for splenomegaly. You start palpating just under the left costal margin and feel nothing.
questions.leadIn: What is the best next step?
options: Start again from the right iliac fossa and move towards the left costal margin
Palpate deep in the left loin bimanually
Percuss over the right costal margin
Roll the patient onto their left side and palpate again
Palpate only while the patient breathes out
questions.explanation: Step 1: recall the direction of growth: the spleen enlarges down and medially along the line of the 10th rib towards the right iliac fossa. Step 2: a very large spleen can therefore fill the abdomen, and if you start under the costal margin your hand may already be on it and miss its edge. Step 3: start in the RIF and work up. If still nothing is felt, lift the lower ribs forward with your left hand and roll the patient onto the right side, then confirm with percussion (Castell spot, Traube space).
whyNot: Deep loin palpation is for the kidney; the spleen is superficial.
The spleen is on the left; percussion at the Castell spot or Traube space is on the left side.
The patient is rolled onto the right side, bringing the spleen forward.
The spleen moves down with inspiration, so ask for a deep breath in; Castell dullness is checked on full inspiration.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old girl has had heavy periods since menarche and frequent nosebleeds. She bled heavily from the start after a tonsillectomy. Her mother has similar problems. Platelet count is normal.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Step 1: read the pattern: mucosal bleeding (nose, periods) and bleeding that starts immediately after surgery mean a primary haemostasis (platelet plug) defect. Step 2: the platelet count is normal, so think of a platelet-adhesion defect. Step 3: she is female with an affected mother, which fits autosomal dominant inheritance, and von Willebrand factor anchors platelets to collagen. Note that routine screening tests can miss von Willebrand disease, so the history is crucial.
whyNot: Haemophilia A is X-linked, so it mainly affects males, and gives delayed, deep bleeding into joints and muscles.
ITP needs a low platelet count; hers is normal.
Vitamin K deficiency is acquired and gives a coagulation pattern, not lifelong mucosal bleeding with a family history.
Scurvy is acquired and dietary; look for perifollicular purpura and gum changes.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 4-year-old boy of Mediterranean origin has severe microcytic anaemia, poor growth, bone deformities and a palpable spleen.
items.explanation: Severe microcytic anaemia in early childhood with failure to thrive, bone deformities and splenomegaly is beta-thalassaemia major; Mediterranean origin supports it.

items.stem: A 60-year-old woman who has had rheumatoid arthritis for many years has recurrent infections, a low neutrophil count, leg ulcers and a palpable spleen.
items.explanation: Rheumatoid arthritis plus splenomegaly plus neutropenia is Felty syndrome.

items.stem: A 22-year-old man has mild jaundice, anaemia and a palpable spleen. His father had his spleen removed for the same condition.
items.explanation: The triad of anaemia, jaundice and splenomegaly is haemolytic anaemia; the family history suggests an inherited cause such as spherocytosis.

items.stem: A 72-year-old man has painless enlarged nodes in his neck, axillae and groins, a modestly enlarged spleen and a raised lymphocyte count.
items.explanation: Generalised lymphadenopathy with lymphocytosis and splenomegaly in an older man points to CLL.

questions.theme: Interpreting a bleeding or clotting history
questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: An 8-year-old girl has a crop of pinpoint, flat, non-blanching spots on her legs and some gum bleeding two weeks after a viral illness. She is otherwise well, with no lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly.
items.explanation: Petechiae in a well child after a viral infection, with no nodes or spleen, fit ITP.

items.stem: A 50-year-old man has repeated nosebleeds, always from the left nostril. His platelet count and clotting tests are normal and he bruises normally.
items.explanation: Recurrent bleeding from one site suggests a local structural lesion rather than a coagulopathy.

items.stem: A 78-year-old woman on long-term anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation has missed her INR checks for two months. She now has a large thigh haematoma and blood in her urine.
items.explanation: Two steps: warfarin needs INR monitoring; without it, over-anticoagulation produces a coagulation-type pattern of deep muscle and genitourinary bleeding.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman has a DVT three months after starting the combined pill. Her brother had a DVT at 28.
items.explanation: Venous thrombosis on the pill with a family history suggests factor V Leiden, which multiplies risk about 100-fold with the pill.

questions.stem: In an OSCE you are asked to examine for epitrochlear lymphadenopathy.
questions.leadIn: Where should you feel for the node?
options: Just above and slightly in front of the medial epicondyle, elbow flexed to 90°
Behind the lateral epicondyle with the elbow straight
In the antecubital fossa over the brachial artery
High on the medial wall of the axilla
questions.explanation: With the elbow flexed to 90°, feel just proximal and slightly anterior to the medial epicondyle. An enlarged epitrochlear node is usually pathological.
whyNot: The epitrochlear node is on the medial side, not the lateral.
The antecubital fossa is not the site of the epitrochlear node.
That is an axillary node site, not the epitrochlear node.
That is where the inguinal nodes lie, along the inguinal ligament.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman has back pain, recurrent pneumonia and anaemia. On examination her tongue is enlarged.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely cause of the enlarged tongue?
questions.explanation: Bone pain, infections and anaemia suggest myeloma, and an enlarged tongue in myeloma reflects amyloidosis.
whyNot: Atrophic glossitis gives a smooth tongue, not an enlarged one.
B12 glossitis gives a smooth, red tongue, not macroglossia.
Leukaemic infiltration causes gum hypertrophy, not tongue enlargement.
HHT gives telangiectasia on the lips and tongue, not enlargement.

questions.theme: Bedside techniques in the haematological examination
questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.
options: Palpation from the right iliac fossa
Rolling the patient onto the right side
Neck examination from behind, patient seated
Epitrochlear palpation with the elbow flexed
Tapping the spine with a closed fist

items.stem: A 66-year-old man with suspected myeloma is examined for marrow expansion while sitting up.
items.explanation: Tap the spine with a fist and press the sternum, clavicles and shoulders; tenderness suggests marrow expansion from myeloma, lymphoma or carcinoma.

items.stem: To percuss for splenomegaly, you percuss the lowest left intercostal space in the anterior axillary line while the patient takes a full breath in.
items.explanation: This is the Castell spot; dullness on full inspiration suggests an enlarged spleen.

items.stem: A 70-year-old woman with Waldenström macroglobulinaemia has headaches and visual blurring. Which examination looks directly for the effect of hyperviscosity?
items.explanation: Hyperviscosity engorges the retinal veins and can lead to papilloedema, seen on fundoscopy.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man of West African origin has recurrent episodes of severe, diffuse bone pain. During an episode his haemoglobin falls and his reticulocyte count rises.
questions.leadIn: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: African origin, diffuse pain crises and a falling Hb with reticulocytosis are the key-word pattern for sickle cell anaemia.
whyNot: Thalassaemia is linked to Mediterranean or southern Asian origin and the trait does not cause pain crises.
Iron deficiency causes low MCV and fatigue, not pain crises with reticulocytosis.
Haemophilia B causes joint and muscle bleeds.
ITP causes petechiae and mucosal bleeding, not bone pain.

questions.stem: An 18-year-old student has had fever and headache for 12 hours. She is drowsy and has a rapidly spreading, non-blanching petechial rash.
questions.leadIn: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A non-blanching petechial rash in an acutely ill, febrile young adult must be treated as meningococcal septicaemia, and petechiae in a young person need immediate hospital assessment.
whyNot: ITP petechiae occur in a well patient, without fever or drowsiness.
HSP gives raised purpura on buttocks and legs, usually without rapid deterioration.
Scurvy is chronic, with perifollicular purpura and gum disease.
Senile purpura occurs in elderly skin with lost elasticity.

ospe.identify: Clinical signs of blood disease: koilonychia (iron deficiency), glossitis and angular stomatitis, gum hypertrophy (AML), petechiae, fundal haemorrhage, toe gangrene (thrombocytosis), swollen haemophilic joint.
Petechial purpura: flat, non-blanching pinpoint skin bleeds → thrombocytopenia.
Digital infarction → think of abnormal globulins such as cryoglobulinaemia.
Prominent scleral (conjunctival) vessels → polycythaemia rubra vera.
Raised purpura on the legs → Henoch–Schönlein purpura (vasculitis, not thrombocytopenia).
Cervical node groups 1–8: submental, submandibular, jugular chain, supraclavicular, posterior triangle, postauricular, preauricular, occipital.
Bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy from the posterior iliac crest under local anaesthetic.
